analytic.title: Work-in-Progress: Response-Time Analysis of Partitioned and Clustered Systems with the Schedule-Abstraction Framework

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The schedule-abstraction framework is a reachability-based response time analysis framework. It was successfully used to analyse many different task models on single core and under global scheduling on multicore. In this work, we extend the schedule-abstraction framework to support the analysis of partitioned and clustered systems where jobs running on different cores, or clusters of cores, have precedence constraints.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Analyzing schedulability and response time in partitioned, clustered and distributed systems is notably difficult when jobs executing on different cores or clusters of cores have precedence constraints [1]. Existing analyses tend to rely on model transformations, where the dependency between jobs assigned on different cores or clusters is modeled as release jitter, offsets or self-suspension delays [1]- [5]. Unfortunately, model transformation are often the cause of a loss of information and thus yield pessimistic analysis results.

As an alternative approach to the typical RTA, the scheduleabstraction framework [6] is a recently developed response time analysis framework that was successfully applied to analyzing global scheduling for various task models (e.g., gang, DAG, self-suspending, EDD, ...) [7]- [10]. It was shown to provide more accurate results than more classical response time analyses [7]- [10]. However, the schedule-abstraction framework is not able to analyse partitioned, clustered or distributed systems yet.

In this work, we extend the schedule-abstraction framework to support the analysis of partitioned and clustered systems where tasks running on different cores or clusters of cores have precedence constraints. We show that a direct extension of the schedule-abstraction framework to partitioned and clustered scheduling leads to a rapid state-space explosion. Then, we present a partial order reduction (POR) technique that exploits information on the independence of scheduling decisions on different clusters to reduce the size of the state-space that needs to be explored during the response-time analysis.

Fig. 1 illustrates the performance differences between the direct and optimized analysis extension presented in this paper. Fig. 1(b) shows an example of five jobs with precedence constraints partitioned across two clusters π 1 and π 2 , each containing a single core. The direct extension of the existing schedule-abstraction framework as presented in Sec. IV, requires to explore 18 system states and analyzes 30 possible scheduling decisions (see Fig. 1(c) where vertices in the graph represent system states and edges represent possible scheduling decisions made by the scheduler). On the other hand, our optimized state-space exploration technique as presented in Sec. V, explores only 8 system states and analyzes only 11 possible (sets of) scheduling decisions (see Fig. 1(d)).
The presented solution is available on GitHub [6].

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: We assume a set of non-preemptive sequential jobs are bounds on the best-case and worst-case execution time of J i , respectively, d i is the absolute deadline of J i , p i is its priority and aff i is the cluster on which J i is assigned to execute (we also call aff i the affinity of J i ). The set of all jobs assigned on cluster π k is thus defined as J k ≜ {∀J i ∈ J | aff i = π k }. A job J i also defines a set pred i ⊆ J containing all jobs that must complete their execution before J i can become ready to execute. We call pred i the set of immediate predecessors of J i , and we call J i a successor of the jobs in pred i . Note that precedence constraints defined by pred i are not limited to jobs with the same affinity than J i . That is, J i may have to wait for jobs assigned to other clusters than aff i before it can start executing. This creates dependencies between the response time analyses on the different clusters.
div.formula: J = {J 1 , J 2 , • • • } executed on a clustered platform. The platform is organized in a set of M virtual or physical clusters Π = {π k | 0 < k ≤ M } where each cluster π k is made of m k identical cores.
div.p: We assume jobs assigned to the same cluster are executed with a work-conserving global job-level fixed priority (JLFP) scheduling policy. A work-conserving JLFP scheduling policy always dispatches the highest-priority ready job whenever a core is free. For ease of notation, we denote the set of jobs with higher priority than a job J i by hp i .

Note that the system model is generic enough that it also allows to model fully partitioned systems (i.e., when there is a single core in each cluster π k ) or global scheduling (i.e., when there is a single cluster made of all cores).
To ease presentation, we assume discrete time, meaning all timing values are integer multiples of a system clock tick.

div.head: III. SCHEDULE ABSTRACTION
div.p: The schedule-abstraction analysis framework as defined in [7], [10] explores the space of all states reachable by the system during execution and checks whether any job may miss its deadline in one of those states. It does so by building a directed acyclic graph G ≜ {V, E} called schedule-abstraction graph (SAG), in which the set of vertices V represents all the states in which the system may be, and the set of directed edges E models the possible transitions between those states. A vertex v ∈ V is an abstract representation of a system state. In this work, we abstract a system state with the following information:

• The set of jobs J v ⊆ J that have already been dispatched until reaching the system state represented by v. • For each job in J v that has a successor that is not dispatched yet, the time interval within which it must have finished its execution. • For each cluster π k , the set of jobs X (c, π k ) that are certainly running on π k in the system state v. • For each cluster π k and for every number of cores p (with 1 ≤ p ≤ m k ), the interval A p (v, π k ) within which p cores of π k become available. We denote the lower and upper bound on that interval by A min p (v, π k ) and A max p (v, π k ), respectively. Those bounds have the following semantics; There are certainly less than p cores free in cluster π k before time A min p (v, π k ). There are certainly at least p cores free in cluster π k at or after time A max p (v, π k ). There are possibly p cores free in cluster π k within the interval
div.formula: A min p (v, π k ), A max p (v, π k ) .
div.p: Based on the information saved in a vertex v, we define the set of jobs that are ready on cluster π k as the set of jobs that were not dispatched yet and that had all their predecessors dispatched until reaching v. We denote that set as
div.formula: R k (v) ≜ {J l | J l ∈ A k \ J v ∧ pred l ⊆ J v }.
div.p: For every job J l ∈ R k (v), we denote the earliest and latest time at which J l becomes ready by ρ min l (v) and ρ max l (v), respectively. The times ρ min l (v) and ρ max l (v) can be calculated with the information saved in v as discussed in [10].

Each edge e ∈ E in the SAG that connects a vertex v ∈ V to another vertex u ∈ V represents a decision by the scheduler to start the execution of a set of jobs S on the platform. The edge e is labelled with the job set S and the earliest and latest time at which each job J i ∈ S will finish its execution when it is dispatched by the scheduler in system state v. The vertex u is then abstracting the system state after the jobs in S have been dispatched in system state v.

A system is said to be schedulable, if the latest finish time of every job J i that was recorded on any edge associated with the dispatch of J i is smaller than J i 's deadline. The best-and worst-case response time of a job J i is the difference between J i 's earliest release time and the smallest, respectively largest, finish time of J i recorded on any edge of the SAG.

div.head: IV. DIRECT EXTENSION TO CLUSTERED SYSTEMS
div.p: Previous works on the schedule abstraction treated the analysis of non-preemptive jobs that are globally scheduled on a multicore platform. Those works explored all possible states reachable by the system by constructing a SAG in a breadth-first manner. In those works, each edge in the SAG represents the dispatch of a single job.

In this section, we extend that approach to the analysis of clustered systems. Since the SAG is built with breadth-first, we use two sets L and L ′ to keep track of all the states in the layer of the SAG that is currently being explored, and in the next layer of the SAG that is currently being built, respectively, (where a layer denotes all vertices at the same given depth).The SAG is then constructed as follows.

1) Start with empty sets L and L ′ . Add an initial vertex to L representing the system state where no job has been dispatched yet on any cluster, i.e., all cores in all clusters are certainly available at time 0. 2) For every state v ∈ L, and for every job J i that was not dispatched yet in v, check if J i may be the first next job dispatched by the scheduler on any cluster (see below for the details). If yes, calculate the earliest and latest finish time of J i assuming it is the next job dispatched in v. Build the new system state u resulting from dispatching J i in v. Add u to L ′ . 3) Once all states in L were explored, if L ′ is not empty, we start exploring the states in L ′ . That is, L ← L ′ , and L ′ ← ∅ and jump back to step 2. Otherwise, all states reachable by the system have been analysed and the construction of the SAG may stop. Checking if a job J i may be the next job dispatched by the scheduler on any cluster (step 2) can be done using the same approach as in [7], [10]. That is, we first calculate an upper bound t wc (v) on the latest time at which a job will certainly be dispatched by the scheduler in system state v (thus J i must start no later than t wc (v) if it is the next job dispatched). Then, we calculate an upper bound t high (v, J i ) on when a job with higher-priority than J i will certainly be ready on the same cluster than J i (J i must then start executing before t high (v, J i ) if it is the next job dispatched by the job-level fixed-priority scheduler). We finally calculate the earliest time EST (v, J i ) at which J i may start to execute in system state v. If EST (v, J i ) ≤ t wc (v) and EST (v, J i ) < t high (v, J i ), then J i may possibly be the next job dispatched by the scheduler.
Slightly modifying the bounds proven in [7], we have:
div.formula: • t wc (v) ≜ min πk∈Π {t k wc (v)} where t k wc (v) ≜ max{A max 1 (v, aff i ), min Jl∈Raff i {ρ max l (v)}}
div.p: is the time at which we certainly have a job ready and a free core on cluster π k . Time t k wc (v) is thus an upper bound on when a job is certainly dispatched by the scheduler on π k .
div.formula: • t high (v, J i ) ≜ min Jh∈Raff i ∩hp i {ρ max h (v)}
div.p: is the time at which a job with higher-priority than J i is certainly ready on cluster π aff i , and
div.formula: • EST (v, J i ) = max{ρ min i , A min 1 (v, aff i )}
div.p: is the earliest time at which J i may be released and a may be free on cluster π aff i . The earliest finish time f min (v, J i ) and latest finish time f max (v, J i ) of a job J i that is dispatched next in system state v is calculated similarly to what is presented in [7], i.e.,
div.formula: f min (v, J i ) = EST (v, J i ) + C min i (1) f max (v, J i ) = min{t wc (v), t high (v, J i ) -1} + C max i (2)
div.p: The new system state resulting from dispatching J i in v is calculated as in [7]. Additionally, to defer the state-space explosion, states with a similar future can also be merged in the SAG. As discussed in [7], [10], two states v and u can be merged if the set of dispatched jobs in v and u is identical and if their core availability intervals overlap or are contiguous.

Example 1: Fig. 1(c) shows the SAG built using the analysis presented above for the five jobs with the parameters and the precedence constraints given in Fig. 1(a)-(b). As can be seen, the SAG analyses a large number of possible orderings of job dispatch decisions that can be taken by the scheduler. For example, it analyses both the dispatch of J 1 followed by J 3 , and J 3 followed by J 1 .
Therefore, even after merging, the number of states explored and the number of edges generated in the SAG grows quickly.

div.head: V. EFFICIENT STATE-SPACE EXPLORATION
div.p: The state-space exploration technique presented in the previous section is inefficient in the sense that it explores many system states containing redundant information.

Example 2: Consider vertices v 2 and v 4 in Fig. 1. The availability intervals of cores in those two states are already captured by the availability intervals in v 6 . Furthermore, one could check that, when applying the equations given in the previous section, the finishing times calculated for J 1 and J 3 does not depend on the path taken to reach v 6 .

To avoid redundant analysis and accelerate the state-space exploration, we observe that in many system states, the next job to be dispatched on some clusters are independent of the jobs that will be dispatched next on other clusters.

Example 3: Consider the initial state v 1 in Fig. 1(c). J 1 and J 2 are the only jobs that may be dispatched on π 1 . Since none of those jobs have predecessors, the time at which they may start executing on π 1 does not depend on the time at which any job is dispatched on π 2 . Similarly, since J 3 and J 4 do not have precedence constraints with jobs on π 1 the time at which one of them will be dispatched on π 2 does not depend on which of J 1 or J 2 is dispatched first on π 1 .

We say that a cluster is independent in system state v if its next job dispatch decision does not dependent on the next dispatch decisions on any other cluster. If multiple clusters are independent in v, sequentially applying dispatch decisions on every independent cluster yields the same state as considering them all at once. Thus, we can skip building intermediate states and directly calculate the final state after a dispatch decision has been made on every independent cluster.
Next, we show how to identify independent clusters and how to use that information to efficiently explore the state-space.

div.head: A. Independence of Cluster Dispatch Decisions
div.p: We explain now how to decide if a cluster π k is independent in a system state v. This is done in two steps. First, for each cluster π k , we identify all jobs assigned to π k that may be the next job dispatched on π k . We denote that job set by N k (v). Then, we check whether the ready time of any job in N k (v) depends on future scheduling decisions on other clusters than π k . If not, then cluster π k is independent in system state v.
To build the set N k (v), we use the properties proven in Lemmas 1 and 2 below.

Lemma 1: A job J i ∈ J may be the next job dispatched by the scheduler on cluster π k in state v only if J i ∈ A k \ J v and r min i ≤ t k wc (v) and pred i ∩ A k ⊆ J v . Proof: To be the next job dispatched on cluster π k , a job J i must respect the following constraints:
1) J i must be assigned to cluster π k and must not have been dispatched yet until reaching system state v, i.e.,
div.formula: J i ∈ A k \ J v . 2) J i must be released before another job is dispatched on π k . Since t k wc (v)
div.p: is an upper bound on when a job is certainly dispatched on π k , it must hold that J i 's earliest release time is no later than t k wc (v), i.e., r min i ≤ t k wc (v). 3) All J i 's predecessors assigned to π k must have been dispatched already. Otherwise, the scheduler must first dispatch the pending predecessors of J i before dispatching J i , in which case J i is not the next job dispatched on π k anymore. That is, we must have pred i ∩ A k ⊆ J v . This proves the lemma.
Note that N k (v) may contain jobs that are not yet ready in system state v due to precedence constraints with jobs assigned to other clusters that have not been dispatched yet.
Lemma 2 further refines the set of jobs that may be in N k (v), identifying jobs that cannot be ready before at least one other job is certainly dispatched on cluster π k .

Lemma 2: A job J i ∈ A k cannot be the next job dispatched on cluster π k in state v if ∃J p ∈ pred i \ J v such that max{ρ min p (v), A min 1 (v, aff p )} + C min p > t k wc (v). Proof: All predecessors of J i must have finished their execution for J i to be dispatched on cluster π k . Let J p ∈ pred i \ J v be one of the predecessors of J i that was not dispatched yet in system state v. The earliest time J p may finish is when it starts at the earliest and executes for its BCET. J p can start executing when it is ready and a core is free in the cluster on which J p is assigned. This happens at the erliest at max{ρ min p (v), A min 1 (v, aff p )}. Thus, J p cannot finish, and consequently J i cannot start, before max{ρ min p (v), A min 1 (v, aff p )} + C min p . Since we know that t k wc (v) is an upper bound on the time at which a job will certainly be dispatched on the cluster π k , we must have
div.formula: max{ρ min p (v), A min 1 (v, aff p )} + C min p ≤ t k wc (v)
div.p: for J i to possibly be the next job dispatched on π k .
Combining Lemmas 1 and 2, we define the set of jobs that can potentially be the next job dispatched on cluster π k as
div.formula: N k (v) ≜ {J i | J i ∈ A k \J v ∧ r min i ≤ t k wc (v) ∧ pred i ∩A k ⊆ J v ∧ ∀J p ∈ pred i \ J v , max{ρ min p (v), A min 1 (v, aff p )} + C min p ≤ t k wc (v)}.
div.p: We then prove in Lemma 3 that a cluster π k is independent in system state v if all the jobs that can potentially be the next job dispatched on cluster π k are ready in system state v.
Lemma 3:
div.formula: A cluster π k ∈ Π is independent in system state v if ∀J i ∈ N k (v), pred i ⊆ J v .
div.p: Proof: By definition of N k (v), the next job dispatched on π k must be one of the jobs in N k (v). Let J i be a job in N k (v). If pred i ⊆ J v , then all predecessors of J i (if it has any) have already been dispatched. Thus, assuming J i is the next job dispatched on π k , J i 's start time cannot be delayed by dispatch decisions made on other clusters. Applying the argument to all jobs in N k (v) proves the lemma.

div.head: B. State-Space Exploration Strategy
div.p: In this section, we explain how we can use our knowledge of independent clusters to accelerate the state-space exploration.

By definition, the next job dispatched on an independent cluster is unaffected by dispatch decisions on other clusters. Say there are n independent clusters in a system state v. Then, the dispatch decisions made by the scheduler on those n independent clusters are independent from one another. We can use that fact by considering the next dispatch decisions on all the n independent clusters in v at once. From the SAG perspective, this means recording the dispatch of n different jobs on a single edge of the graph outgoing from v (for example, see vertex v 2 in Fig. 1(d)).
Dispatching n jobs at once allows to fast forward the statespace exploration, avoiding the exploration of all intermediate states resulting from dispatching jobs in any possible ordering.

To fully exploit the properties of independent clusters and improve the efficiency of the state-space exploration when building the SAG, the exploration algorithm is modified to only dispatch jobs on independent clusters when expending a state. That is, considering a system state v in which there is at least one independent cluster, there is no outgoing edge from v labeled with the dispatch of a job on a cluster that is not independent. If there is no independent cluster in v, then we follow the same procedure described in Sec. IV where all possible dispatch decisions on all clusters are explored.

As shown in Fig. 1(d), favoring dispatch on independent clusters allows to quickly fast-forward in the SAG (i.e, only the red vertices of Fig. 1(c) are built in Fig. 1(d)). This avoids exploring many possible dispatch orderings that all eventually result in the same system state. Another advantage of favoring the the exploration of the impact of dispatch decisions on independent clusters first, is that the system state resulting from the dispatch decisions made on the independent clusters may reveal the independence of other clusters, for example, by bringing to light that predecessors of a job assigned to a cluster π k cannot finish before t k wc (v) (see Lemma 2).

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we presented how the the schedule-abstraction framework can be extended to analyse the response time of partitioned and clustered systems. We proposed a POR technique to reduce the number of system states that must be explored during the analysis. We showed by means of an example that the proposed POR technique may drastically reduce the size of the SAG built during the analysis in comparison to a solution that does not exploit information about independent scheduling decisions on different clusters. The solution presented in this paper was implemented in the public version of the schedule-abstraction framework and is now available on GitHub [6].
